G:cross_family:0.teen_blockers: Age: not a legal wall. He is an adult and can form an LLC, sign contracts and take payments. Licenses: none needed while the product stays non-advice and non-brokering. Legal walls that are real but clearable by design: (1) Fla. Stat. 817.505 patient brokering covers AHCA-licensed home health agencies and carries felony penalties ($50k up to $500k), so per-start fees to agencies must be dropped; a flat fair-market fee to a non-steering consumer information service fits exemption (3)(i). (2) Florida Bar Rule 4-7.22 makes CareFund a 'qualifying provider' for lawyers: no fee-sharing, a panel with lawyers from at least 4 firms, annual list to the Bar, 15-day written response; this conflicts with the '2 attorneys' start and the 'exclusive county' offer. (3) SEC Marketing Rule 206(4)-1: any advisor paying per referral makes CareFund a paid promoter (written agreement, disclosure at referral, eligibility checks); SmartAsset shows it is workable and Dad's compliance toolkit is a real edge. (4) HIPAA marketing rule: an agency handout promoting a third-party advisor funded directly or indirectly by that advisor likely needs patient authorization; keep no remuneration to agencies and no PHI. (5) VA: no claim-prep fees unless accredited. Capital: legal review pushes cost to about $6-10k, not $4k. Unverified and load-bearing: nothing public confirms what MHC Healthcare is (only an unverified 'MHC Area 6 LLC' Riverview listing on a low-quality directory), and MyFinancialAdvice looks like a small Boulder CO firm founded 2001 (about 8 employees per one profile, last detailed coverage 2004), so Dad's 'advisor roster' may be thin. sharpened.pitch: Families learn private-duty care costs about $6,000 a month in a crisis; most then cut hours or never convert from a Medicare episode. Agencies lose the conversion, and attorneys and advisors meet the family late. CareFund is a non-advice intake agencies hand out at admission and discharge. It produces a funding map (LTC policy claim checklist, VA Aid and Attendance, Medicaid waiver, state programs, family cost-sharing) and a booked consult with a vetted professional. Three changes from the original. First, the payers change: elder-law attorneys (a rotating panel of four or more per county, flat monthly sponsorship) and hybrid or AUM advisors under written promoter agreements pay, because a roughly $300 flat-fee consult cannot carry a $200-350 lead fee; flat-fee planners become the low-cost tier. Agencies pay a small flat fair-market license, with no per-start fees. Second, the family-agency pilot is instrumented, together with three or four free peer pilots using de-identified aggregates, to produce the one number peers will pay for: private-pay conversion and length-of-stay lift. Third, the product that scales is the compliance rail itself (SEC promoter agreements and disclosures, Florida Bar 4-7.22 panel rules, HIPAA marketing guardrails, built from Dad's compliance tooling), which carriers, banks and caregiver-benefit vendors need more than another lead list. Kill criteria: by April 2027, if fewer than 3 of 10 peer agencies would pay $300 a month after seeing pilot data, stop.

G:insider_big:1.teen_blockers: Age and legal form are not blockers: he is 18 and can form an LLC, sign contracts and take payments. No license wall exists, because grading AI outputs on synthetic prompts is not giving regulated medical or financial advice. The blockers that are real: (1) Credibility. Vendors will ask who the clinical lead is. He needs a named credentialed lead, such as an MHC director of nursing or an HHCS-O auditor, and fixable. (2) Independence conflict. If MHC is a customer or affiliate of a vendor he grades, 'independent' is compromised. MHC Area 9 LLC is registered as doing business as Choice Health At Home, which is acquiring Accentra, whose CEO created the Apricot AI tool. This is unverified and the single biggest unknown. (3) Bench existence. The family company may have sold its agencies to Choice, in which case the RN/coder bench may not be his to recruit. The only exact-name search hit for MHC Healthcare was an unrelated Arizona nonprofit, and MyFinancialAdvice shows only 2004-era press, so the advisor network's current state is unverified. (4) HIPAA. Low while everything is synthetic, but it becomes real if experts write charts from memory of real patients or if retainer evals run on production traces. (5) Worker classification. Minor at under 10 project-based experts, but a real wall at scale: Mercor (Texas), Handshake (N.D. Cal., July 2026) and Scale (SF) are all being sued over AI-trainer misclassification. (6) Expert-data security. The Mercor breach (March 2026) led to at least 4-7 class actions. (7) Advisor side-gigs. FINRA 3270 requires registered reps to give prior written notice to their firm, so flat-fee RIAs are lighter. (8) Capital at scale: experts are paid weekly before clients pay, so a $50M-billing marketplace needs a multi-million float, but the pilot needs under $10k.

The better payer is the agency or advisor firm choosing a vendor, not the vendor itself: only 1.3% of 160 agency respondents were 'very confident' in their OASIS accuracy, and CMS leaves coding liability with the agency.
G:insider_big:1.deciding_reason: The wedge is real but too small, and the only big path is a fight with Mercor. I found no independent accuracy benchmark for AI OASIS vendors and no home-health-specific bench, and there is no license or age wall. But the vertical is about 80 named AI vendors, which bottoms up to $1-3M a year, not the pitch's $5-15M. The generic expert-eval lane is occupied: Mercor now sells Enterprise Evals to application-layer companies (Ramp, Cognition) from a 30k-expert, $2B-run-rate base, and Centaur and Vals already own the healthcare and independent-benchmark niches. The vendor-pays model has a structural problem: vendors want badges, not honest scores, in-house clinical teams do it today (Hippocratic, Ada), and CHAI's assurance-lab plan failed partly because nobody settled who pays. The $2,500 price is below the roughly $5-6k build cost of a defensible 100-chart gold set, so the first pilots lose money. The idea survives as weak, not dead, because the buyer side (agencies, with 1.3% confidence in OASIS accuracy and liability under CMS) is unserved and KLAS shows a $40M-scale vendor-funded ratings model exists, but that path takes years and needs a verified MHC bench.

sharpened.title: Ground Truth Ledger: the independent accuracy scoreboard for back-office AI in regulated services
sharpened.one_liner: A small credentialed bench grades back-office AI (home-health OASIS first, advisor communications second) on hidden synthetic gold sets, sells blind diagnostics and buyer-side vendor bake-offs, then turns the accumulated rubrics and an anonymized index into a subscription standard that vendors license a verified badge from.
sharpened.pitch:
The weak point of the original idea was the payer and the scale model. Vendors will not pay for honest independent scores, and a 2,000-expert marketplace is a head-on fight with Mercor, which now sells enterprise evals from a 30,000-expert, roughly $2B-run-rate base. The sharpened version keeps the expert bench but changes who pays and what is sold.

Step 1, days 0-90: build one 100-chart synthetic OASIS gold set with a hidden test split, graded by three credentialed coders with inter-annotator agreement and an error taxonomy. His pipelines pre-grade, cutting expert time by roughly 60-70%. Sell a $5,000 blind diagnostic to vendors. The first two go for $2,500 as design partners, with testimonial and anonymized-publication rights, since a defensible set costs about $5-6k to build.

Step 2: sell a buyer-side bake-off to agencies choosing among AI vendors, at $3-10k. Only 1.3% of 160 surveyed agencies were very confident in their OASIS accuracy, CMS leaves coding liability with the agency, and no independent benchmark exists. This is the payer with the mandate and the pain.

Step 3, months 6-24: publish an anonymized industry accuracy index. Vendors that score well license a verified badge, and gold sets and rubrics are sold as subscriptions. KLAS, at roughly $40M of revenue, shows that vendor-funded independent ratings can last, so the moat is a data asset and a standard, not a take-rate on hours.

Step 4: advisor-AI marketing-rule and client-communication review only after a signed design partner from his father's network.

Gate zero, before spending a dollar: confirm what MHC Healthcare actually is. Its Florida entities appear to operate under Choice Health At Home, which is tied to Apricot, a vendor he would grade. An independence conflict, or a sold company with no bench, changes the plan. Keep the bench to 10-20 people on per-project contracts through a payroll partner.

G:mhc_revenue:0.teen_blockers: Age: not a blocker. He is 18 and can form an LLC, sign BAAs and fee agreements, and take payments. License: I found no license required to audit remits or file payer disputes on an agency's behalf, but a healthcare attorney must confirm. That is a roughly $2-3k check; the estimate is mine. Credibility: real for non-family owners and not real for the family pilot. Strangers will want a result from the family agency, so the first 3 peers must come through the grandfather's calls. A cold 18-year-old pitching contract audits to owners will not close. Legal wall 1, Medicare billing-agent rule: 42 CFR 424.73(b)(3) bars an agent's pay from being tied to dollars billed or collected, but only for agents who receive Medicare payments. It is not triggered if all cash goes to the agency's own accounts and he never touches funds. Real but avoidable. Legal wall 2, Florida Medicaid: Fla. Stat. 409.913 (subsection number unconfirmed) reportedly bars percentage pay to billing agents on Medicaid claims. Medicaid managed-care work must be flat-fee. Real but avoidable. Legal wall 3, anti-kickback: OIG treats percentage billing pay as a risk because it can encourage upcoding. A pure contract-rate audit has less of that risk, and a lawyer must sign off before any fee agreement. Real but clearable. HIPAA: a BAA with every customer and a sub-BAA with the model vendor. Anthropic offers an API BAA and zero retention, but one June 2026 secondary source says its newest 'Covered' models require 30-day retention and cannot run under zero-retention. Verify directly before touching PHI. Real but manageable. Scaling blocker: beyond the family and 3-5 friendly owners, chains will demand SOC 2, cyber and E&O insurance. That is real and costs money and months, but it does not block the first 60-90 days. Biggest unverified premise: MHC Healthcare as an owner-operated home-health company. Directory listings show 'MHC Area 6/9/10 LLC' as Medicare-certified Florida agencies (Riverview, Boca Raton dba Choice Health At Home, Fort Lauderdale) with no owner named. Nothing I found ties Peremel to MHC. If the family firm is not a home-health operator with Medicare Advantage revenue, the pilot and the trust advantage vanish.

The January 2027 rate-change window is a talking point only, because I found no source that plans load rates late. Associations are too slow for the 6-month goal. HomeCareCon (Home Care Association of Florida) was July 21-24, 2026 and the next is July 2027. The Alliance for Care at Home webinar series is policy-focused with no revenue-cycle session found. First 10: (1) the family group (the MHC Area N agencies, if verified). (2-4) Three Florida owner-peers the grandfather calls personally, preferably multi-location groups. (5-6) Two Home Care Association of Florida member groups reached through a grandfather or mentor introduction, using a short written scan offer. (7-8) Two healthcare CPA or attorney firms serving agencies, as referral channels only, with no referral fees until counsel reviews. (9) One PE-backed regional operator via the mentor's network. (10) One billing company or EHR reseller that wants a premium add-on. Target groups with $10M+ of non-FFS revenue, not $3M single agencies.
G:mhc_revenue:0.deciding_reason: The idea reaches a first paying customer and clears the legal walls, but the home-health-only fee pool is too small for $10M a year and the leakage rate is unproven. Size: MedPAC reports $16.0B of fee-for-service home health spend in 2024 across 12,234 agencies. Using SimiTree's 26% MA revenue share (2022) and a growing MA share since, MA home-health revenue is about $8-10B. That is well below the idea's $12-16B. Public leakage anchors are 0.5-1% of net patient revenue (R1, hospitals) and 1-3% (a vendor webinar, commercial payers). Applying 1% leakage and 60% recoverable, with a 25% fee, gives a national fee pool of about $12-15M. Even the idea's own 3% leakage gives only about $40-50M. $10M a year therefore needs 70-80% of the base pool, or 20-25% of the optimistic pool. An agency with $3M of MA revenue yields only about $4-9k a year in fees. A realistic median is about $0.4M a year by year 3. Only a pooled payer benchmark, or expansion into hospice, SNF and outpatient lines, gets near $6M. Those lines are crowded with funded rivals (Fuse, Trek, R1, Aspirion, Ensemble). The January rate-reset premise is also thin. No source supports plans loading rates late. The CY2027 proposed update is +2.4%, so a 60-90 day lag would be worth only about 0.4-0.6% of percent-of-Medicare revenue. CY2026 was a -1.3% cut, which makes late loading overpay the agency. Incumbent check: no one is doing home-health-specific MA contract-compliance recovery, but HHAeXchange (April 2026) already lists underpayment recovery under contract management, and Claim Health, Fuse and Trek could add the feature. Cost, legal and reach are fine. Size and an unproven leakage rate are the problem. Run it as a 30-day, near-zero-cost test on the family's remits, not as the company.

sharpened.title: Payer Truth for Multi-Site Post-Acute Operators: contract-compliance recovery plus a payer scorecard
sharpened.one_liner: Free 30-day scan of a multi-site home-health group's remittances against its signed payer contracts, 20-25% contingency on recovered Medicare Advantage and commercial dollars, and a pooled payer-performance index that becomes the real asset.
sharpened.pitch: Payer Truth is a contract-compliance audit and payer scorecard for multi-site home-health operators. Under a BAA, it ingests twelve months of remittances (835s) plus the signed Medicare Advantage, commercial and VA contracts. It recomputes what each claim should have paid (percent-of-Medicare PDGM, per-visit or per-episode) and files dispute packets citing contract sections inside each plan's window. The agency's own bank account receives all money, so the Medicare billing-agent rule is never triggered. MA and commercial recoveries carry a 20-25% fee, subject to attorney review. Medicaid managed-care work is flat-priced because Florida reportedly bars percentage billing-agent pay on Medicaid claims. The wedge is a free scan of the family group's remits with a pre-registered rule: at least 1.0% of MA revenue recoverable means build; 0.5-1.0% means turn it into a benchmark product; under 0.5% means stop. Customers are groups with $10M+ of non-FFS revenue (an unverified guess of 150-300 operators nationally), not $3M single agencies, which yield only $4-9k a year in fees. Each audit adds to a pooled payer-performance index: share of contract rate actually paid, days to pay and appeal overturn rates by plan and county. That index is the only asset that can reach $10M, sold to PE-backed operators, lenders and buyers as payer-mix diligence during home-health deals. Home-health audits alone cap at roughly $5-15M of fees nationwide.

sharpened.pitch:
Florida's independent home-health owners are squeezed three ways. Medicare has had four straight permanent cuts and faces a proposed temporary minus 3 percent for 2027. A federal enrollment freeze blocks new branches. And Medicare Advantage rates are set in private contracts that nobody publishes, because MA plans sit outside the Transparency in Coverage rule. Each owner negotiates alone against Humana's CenterWell and against plan-side network managers like Tango.

The Alliance starts where the family's convening power is strongest and antitrust risk is lowest: a quarterly owners' roundtable chaired by the grandfather, under written, counsel-reviewed ground rules, with no rate talk in the room. Members pay for something private. Each agency uploads its MA contracts and remittances under a BAA, stripped to payer, code, units, paid amount and county, and gets an audit of paid versus contracted rates. It reuses the contract-versus-invoice engine Asher already built for freight. The fee is flat plus a share of recovered underpayments. MHC's own remits are the first test, and the idea is dropped if leakage is under about 0.5 percent of MA revenue.

Only after that data exists does the Alliance build the shared layer. First an aggregated MA rate cube, released on counsel's rules: at least five contributors per cell, none over 25 percent, data at least three months old, no price recommendations. Then group purchasing under the 3 percent safe harbor. Payer contracting comes last, and only through a licensed clinically integrated network partner. The Home Care Association of Florida is the partner, not the rival, and the model then repeats with other state associations and extends to hospice.

sharpened.title: Audit Packet: the counsel-ready evidence layer for Medicare home health and hospice
sharpened.one_liner: A continuously maintained, audit-ready file for every billed period, covering certification, plan of care, face-to-face, orders and signature order, plus visit-presence and authenticity evidence, so an ADR, pre-claim submission or UPIC request is answered from the file in a day, sold through counsel and priced on revenue at risk.
sharpened.pitch: Medicare's own Florida denial data (Palmetto, Apr-Jun 2026) shows what actually costs agencies money: no plan of care or certification (34%), records not submitted (24%), face-to-face not met (14%), medical necessity (11%) and missing orders. Visits billed but not documented are only 5.5%. So Audit Packet leads with completeness. For every billed 30-day period it keeps a live evidence file that checks the cert, plan of care, F2F, orders, signature and date order, and that the record can be produced inside the 30-45 day ADR window. It then attaches visit-presence evidence from the EMR and EVV (timestamps, GPS, mileage, duration versus note length) reconciled to the notes. The similarity and authorship queue from his detector is one module, a needs-review queue with per-agency template baselines and never an accusation. It is sold two ways: directly to agencies at roughly 0.5% of Medicare revenue (about $8-12 per paid period, $6-9k a year for a typical agency; assumption), and through two or three Florida fraud-defense firms who retain it under privilege, so findings do not start an unprivileged 60-day overpayment clock. Engagement fees run $2-10k per UPIC or TPE response. The moat is not a pooled PHI corpus, which owners and BAAs resist. It is a published, pre-registered validation of false-positive rates, with a credentialed statistician and a certified coder as advisors, so UPIC and ALJ readers give the packet weight. It is built to be EMR-agnostic where Brellium and the EMRs are not. The design forbids any feature that helps rewrite notes to evade detection. Start with a free scan of MHC's labeled set after confirming MHC is a Medicare HHA, then a paid $2-4k pilot. Kill if precision on the DON-labeled set is under 70%, if it surfaces nothing that MHC's real ADR/TPE history confirms, or if fewer than two of five warm non-family owners or counsel pay for a retro scan within 30 days. Then expand to hospice and Medicaid EVV reconciliation.

G:mhc_revenue:1.deciding_reason: CMS's own burden numbers (4,700 agencies, 1,600,608 hours a year, about 340 hours per agency) put the whole RCD paperwork labor pool near $42M, not the pitch's $150M ($35K per agency is about 3.5x too high), and Palmetto medical-review denials number only about 334 to 1,206 per quarter across six states. So $10M a year is about 17% of the entire pool even at 100% outsourcing, and RCD sunsets around May 2029. SimiTree, Enzo, Forcura, Axxess and offshore virtual assistants already cover the work, and the 50-state order-release network second act is Forcura's and Enzo's turf. Several why-now claims are also wrong or stale: the 84.4% figure blends pre-claim (97% affirmed) with postpayment, F2F is now only 10-14% of denials after the CY2026 rule widened who can perform it, and the 45-day OASIS claim is unverified. It is not kill because the family test bed is real, unsigned orders and unanswered records requests do drive the largest denial categories (up to 34% and 44% in single quarters), nothing legal blocks him, and an outsourced per-result order-release desk was not found.

sharpened.title: Signed-Order Release Desk: held claims to cash for home health and hospice
sharpened.one_liner: An EHR-agnostic order-chase and records-response layer, priced per claim released, that targets the two failures behind most 2026 Palmetto denials (missing plan-of-care or certification signatures and unanswered records requests), with the Review Choice packet check as the free lead-in.
sharpened.pitch:
Medicare will not let a home health agency bill a period until every order in it is signed, and Palmetto's recent denial data shows the same two failures again and again: no plan of care or certification (18 to 34 percent of medical-review denials by quarter) and requests for records that were never answered (24 to 44 percent). Neither is a clinical judgment problem. Both are chase problems: a physician who has not signed, an agency that missed a deadline. Today an agency solves them with a full-time order coordinator, an offshore virtual assistant, or software inside its EHR that only works if the physician cooperates.

The Signed-Order Release Desk is an EHR-agnostic layer that chases every unsigned order by fax, text and e-sign link, tracks a signature-turnaround scorecard per physician, and answers records requests before the clock runs out. Billing is a flat fee per claim released, never a percentage, so it stays clear of the billing-agent rule. Review Choice packet checks are the free lead-in that earns access to the aging report.

Start with the family agency's held-claims aging report and baseline days-to-signature as the proof. Pitch Florida peers in postpayment review first, because they are the ones struggling to reach 90 percent. Then take it to hospice and to the other 49 states, where orders work the same way. Staff it with a bench of contract RNs, not a teenager reading charts, and treat Forcura and Enzo as partners or acquirers rather than rivals to out-build. Be honest that the ceiling is a few million dollars a year unless the cross-EHR physician scorecard becomes a real data asset.

G:insider_personas:3.teen_blockers:
Age is not a legal blocker. He is 18 and a HIPAA business associate has no age rule. No licence is needed to sell software or QA to covered entities, so that wall is not real. Capital is not a blocker either (about $4k).

Credibility is real. Buyers' counsel will hesitate to hand PHI and False Claims Act exposure to a teenager with no CPC, HCS-D or RN credentials.

The legal premise is real. An outside audit that finds overpayments is credible information under the 60-day rule (reasonable diligence, then repay within 60 days, 6-year lookback). Calling it coaching does not avoid that. Buyers will want a lawyer to retain him for privilege, and I found no authority on whether his work product would be protected.

HIPAA friction is real but clearable. Every customer, MHC included, needs a BAA. Using Claude on charts needs Anthropic's BAA plus a zero-data-retention organization arranged through sales. One third-party source says Claude Code is not covered, which I did not confirm on Anthropic's own page. Running the similarity and stylometry locally avoids this.

False-positive risk is real. No study I found measures AI-text detector false positives on short, templated clinical notes. A per-clinician machine-authorship list invites HR and defamation problems.

MHC is unverified. Directory listings show MHC AREA 6 LLC and MHC AREA 10 LLC as Medicare-certified home health agencies, but nothing links them to his grandfather. A paid pilot from a family company is also weak evidence that the market will pay. The mentor founded an audio-visual integration company, so the PE-healthcare introductions are unproven.
G:insider_personas:3.first_customers_channel:
Realistic channel: his grandfather's circle of Florida home-health and hospice owners, plus one healthcare compliance attorney who retains him for privilege. Expect 3 to 6 paying customers in 6 months at best. The state associations are weak channels because Brellium already shows the Florida Hospice & Palliative Care Association and the Texas Association for Home Care & Hospice as customer logos.

First 10 named customer types:

2-4. Three Florida home-health owner-operators from his grandfather's peer circle.

G:insider_personas:3.deciding_reason: Both halves of the product are already sold by funded companies with real customers. Brellium sells copy-paste and boilerplate note detection to agencies, including the associations in the plan, and Codoxo has sold cloning and partial-AI-generation detection to payer SIUs since March 2026. The one piece nobody sells, AI-authorship detection for a provider, has no buyer, because the agency's own scribe and EHR logs already show which notes are AI-written. The problem pitch is also thin: the Palmetto denial rankings I found are dominated by face-to-face, missing-record and plan-of-care issues, not cloned visit notes. Reaching $10M a year would take about 7% of all 12,234 Medicare HHAs, in a segment where Brellium, Enzo and the EHR vendors already sell.

sharpened.title: Chart Provenance: independent documentation-authenticity diligence for post-acute deals and audits
sharpened.one_liner: A neutral third-party forensic check on whether a home health or hospice agency's charts show real, individualized care, sold to acquirers, lenders, insurers and counsel who must rely on the records but do not control the EHR.
sharpened.pitch: Brellium sells to the agency and Codoxo sells to the payer. Neither sells to the third party in the middle, who needs an opinion from someone other than the agency or the agency's own vendor. With new Medicare home health and hospice enrollments frozen since 13 May 2026, the only way into the business is to buy an existing licence, and the freeze can be extended in 6-month steps. Acquirers, their lenders and their R&W/E&O insurers then need to know whether a target's charts are genuine or full of cloned and machine-filled documentation. Healthcare counsel responding to an ADR or UPIC request needs the same check. Asher sells a sampled forensic report, 300 to 500 charts, at roughly $5 to 15k per deal. It combines corpus-level cross-patient and cross-clinician clone statistics, his gestalt and compare-drafts method, scribe and EHR provenance logs, and timestamp and mileage reconciliation. A healthcare lawyer retains him so the work is privileged, and MHC is the lab under a BAA. The path to something large is a benchmark: a cross-agency integrity baseline that lenders and insurers adopt as a standard. That is unproven, and Codoxo's payer-side position is the main threat. Before building anything, he should call 10 healthcare M&A advisors and attorneys over two weeks at no cost. If fewer than 3 say they would pay $5k or more, he should kill this too.

G:mhc_workforce:2.teen_blockers: Age: not a legal blocker (18, can contract; this is B2B). Credibility: partly real. HIPAA: mostly avoided; recruiting data is HR data. Capital: not a blocker (~$3k). MHC ownership and its aide-hiring volume are unverified.

ComForCare Miami Lakes pays a $250 referral bonus after 250 hours, a price anchor for what agencies already pay.
G:mhc_workforce:2.deciding_reason: The fee is contingent on 90-day retention, a variable the recruiter does not control, and the plan sources from the worst-retention channels: Activated Insights 2026 shows social-media-sourced caregivers at 107% turnover and word of mouth at 77%, versus 65.8% for an agency's own website. The Haiti TPS ending on 27 Jul 2026 shrinks the Creole-speaking work-authorized pool the funnel draws on. Cheap substitutes exist: about $113-250 of ads per hire and $720-1,865/mo done-for-you vendors. Cash per start is only about $510-690, which leaves thin gross margin. Bottom-up the realistic market is $1-2M a year in the tri-county area, and $10M+ needs multi-state reach with an operations-heavy business. The upsides are real: the family pilot pays within about 8 weeks, there is no license wall for W-2 recruiting, and HIPAA is mostly avoided.

sharpened.title: Day-90 Aide Network: school-sourced bilingual aides with a first-90-days concierge, priced on retention
sharpened.one_liner: Florida home-care agencies pay about $900 per aide only if the aide is still working on day 90. We source credentialed aides from HHA/CNA training programs and community channels, run Creole, Spanish and English check-ins through the first 90 days, and own the retention data.
sharpened.pitch:
Home-care agencies lose about three of every four aides a year, and half of the departures happen in the first three months. Recruiters sell them applicants; nobody is paid for the aide who is still there at day 90. Day-90 Aide Network is paid that way: $300 when the aide starts, $600 at day 90 (price-tested against a higher credentialed-bilingual tier), with one free replacement.

Three changes make the pricing defensible instead of reckless. First, we source mainly from HHA and CNA training programs, adult-ed centers and workforce boards, which produce credentialed candidates and want placement statistics, and use WhatsApp, Facebook groups, churches and radio for reach. The 2026 benchmark shows social-media-sourced aides turn over at 107%, so social cannot be the only source. Second, we own the variable we are paid on: a Creole, Spanish and English check-in line at days 3, 14, 30 and 60, with escalation to the agency. The contract sets a minimum of offered weekly hours and payroll proof, so we are not paid for outcomes the agency can sabotage. Third, we never screen immigration documents. The agency runs I-9 and E-Verify (Florida requires it at 25+ employees), candidates are told the requirement upfront, and a lawyer reviews the flow before the first ad.

The first customer is MHC, as a measured pilot of 10-20 hires that yields survival curves by channel and by agency. That data is what peer agencies will buy, and the opted-in candidate base becomes the asset that feeds Day-One Desk. Surge Bench waits until an AHCA health care services pool registration is filed. Scaling means other metros and other language communities (Spanish, Creole, Cape Verdean, Tagalog), toward a retained-hire marketplace for frontline care workers.

G:mhc_coo:4.teen_blockers: Age: none legally (adult, can form an LLC, sign contracts, take payments). Credibility is the real blocker: compliance officers and healthcare attorneys will not take an 18-year-old cold, so a grandfather or mother introduction is the only route (real, mitigable only through family). License: no licence wall for software, but unauthorized-practice-of-law risk is real if the tool says 'compliant' or applies law itself; manageable by applying only client-set thresholds and getting counsel to review the template and terms (about $1.5-2.5k). HIPAA: avoid PHI so no BAA is needed (real design constraint, not a wall). Capital: about $3k to first revenue is fine; SOC 2 (roughly $10-25k) will be asked by chains around month 6-12 (real for non-family scale). Governance: MHC ownership and type are unverified (public record shows MHC Area 6/9/10 LLC home-health agencies); the family pilot proves little independently, and a ledger is a discoverable record that MHC counsel may resist if past practice was unlogged. Father's tech edge is weak: MyFinancialAdvice shows 8 employees and no listed customers on Gust and its website was unreachable; the architecture is commodity.
G:mhc_coo:4.first_customers_channel: Channel: grandfather and mother introductions at MHC first, then peer owner-operators, with healthcare compliance attorneys as the recommending channel and the Home Care Association of Florida (HomeCareCon), Florida Alliance for Home Care Services and the Florida Hospice and Palliative Care Association (FHPCA; Associate $600/yr, Patron $3,200/yr) for reach. First 10 named customer types: (1) MHC corporate marketing and liaison team plus its compliance lead (design partner); (2) other MHC Area LLC locations; (3) grandfather's peer owner-operated Florida home-health agencies in the same AHCA regions; (4) multi-location Florida home-health operators; (5) for-profit Florida hospice operators (only about 45 Florida hospices exist, so this segment is tiny); (6) PE-backed Florida home-health roll-ups; (7) Florida healthcare compliance attorneys who write client gift policies (referral partners and resellers); (8) outsourced compliance consultants such as SimiTree (channel partners); (9) Home Care Association of Florida member agencies; (10) specialty pharmacy and DME operators as the first adjacent vertical.
G:mhc_coo:4.deciding_reason: The empty niche is empty because it is small and already substituted. About 18,900 Medicare-certified agencies (12,234 home health plus 6,706 hospices, 2024) sit on margins where roughly 48% of home-health agencies were projected negative. Full compliance suites sell for $99-$519 a month, so a single-function $400-$900 a month tool is priced above them, and the pitched $9k a year needs about 1,100 customers at 2-4x the benchmark price. The product's core is weaker than pitched: the AKS has no gift safe harbor and Florida 817.505 exempts conduct the AKS permits, so thresholds are client-set (only the $535 Stark cap for physicians is a hard number), which makes the engine a log, a cap cell and a sign-off that Excel, Ramp-style policy agents, hospital NMC trackers and GRC gift registers already cover. Recent Florida patient-brokering prosecutions are sober homes and labs, and 2025-26 hospice and home-health settlements (Creative Hospice $9.2M, Traditions $34M) are about medical-director payments, not meals. Median is about $0.7M a year and upside about $8M, below the $10M bar, so the standalone gift ledger fails the 'defensible and big' rule. It survives only as a cheap 60-day test with MHC as design partner and a widened product.

sharpened.title: Referral Remuneration Ledger for Post-Acute Care
sharpened.one_liner: One system of record for everything of value that flows to anyone who can steer a patient to a home-health or hospice agency: gifts, meals, free in-services, medical-director agreements with time logs and fair-market-value evidence, marketer pay structures and sponsorships, checked against counsel-set policy and the current Stark cap and attested monthly.
sharpened.pitch: Home-health and hospice agencies live on referrals, and every referral source is a potential Anti-Kickback or Florida patient-brokering problem. Today the control is a compliance officer's spreadsheet plus a card statement. The Referral Remuneration Ledger replaces that with one audit-ready system of record. It logs every item of value given to a physician, discharge planner or facility: meals, gifts, events, free in-services and free staff time. It also holds the contracts that actually drove the recent nine- and eight-figure settlements: medical-director agreements with time logs and third-party fair-market-value opinions, marketer pay structures and sponsorships. Thresholds are set by each client's counsel, with the current Stark cap ($535 in 2026) updated yearly, and the software applies them without giving legal advice or ever calling anything compliant. Items route to supervisory review, staff attest monthly, and the archive is firewalled from patient and referral-volume data so it cannot become evidence of intent. Sell per location (about $250 a month, with chain pricing) through healthcare attorneys and the Florida home-care and hospice associations, with MHC as the design partner and first paying customer. Widening from gifts to arrangements moves the product to the hospital-style NMC and contract tools (MedPro, symplr, RLDatix) that no one has built for post-acute, lifts the budget line and gives a path to about 1,500 locations and roughly $8M a year. It is unproven. Test in 30 days: ten calls (MHC marketing and compliance, five owner peers, three attorneys). Kill it if marketers will not log, attorneys do not want a discoverable record, buyers say Excel plus an expense tool is enough, or a referral CRM ships the feature.

G:mhc_revenue:3.teen_blockers:
Age is not a blocker: he is 18 and can form an LLC, sign contracts and sign a BAA. No Florida billing-agent licence turned up in my searches (not exhaustively checked). Four walls are real.
1. REAL, fatal to the model. The freight-style fee of a percentage of recovered dollars is barred for anyone who prepares or helps with a Medicaid claim. Fla. Stat. 409.913(10) says billing-agent pay may not be based on amounts billed or on what the provider receives from Medicaid. 42 CFR 447.10(f) says pay must be related to processing cost, not related on a percentage or other basis to amounts billed or collected, and not dependent on collection. The $8-15 per resolved visit fallback is still risky if 'resolved' means paid. Only a flat monthly or per-packet-filed fee is clean, so get a healthcare attorney's opinion.
2. REAL. Credibility and PHI. Agency owners hand claims data and portal logins to a teenager only after a BAA, E&O and cyber insurance, and references. HHAeXchange is the gatekeeper and no public Florida provider API exists. Sharing agency logins is a security and terms problem.
3. REAL, new. The family pilot is unverified. The CMS NPI registry lists MHC Area 3, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10, LLC as home health, all with the other name Choice Health at Home. Their authorized official is Katrina Lanier, with a Tyler, TX mailing address. MHC Area 7 is Haven Home Health Care. Choice Health at Home is a PE-backed national company (Trive Capital, Coltala) built on Medicare Advantage, not an owner-operated family firm. Either the family's MHC is a different company or it sold. A skilled Medicare or MA agency would also have a small SMMC Medicaid book.
4. PARTLY REAL. False Claims Act exposure. Tools that help appeal visits with no EVV, or with edited times, can drift into helping bill unverified services.
G:mhc_revenue:3.first_customers_channel: Channel: warm introductions through the family (only after confirming what MHC is), the Home Care Association of Florida (HomeCareCon, Orlando, July 2027) and its member agencies, nurse-registry owners found through AHCA HealthFinder, and the Florida LTC plan network directories (Sunshine, Molina, Humana, Aetna). First 10 customer types: (1) the family agency if it has a Medicaid book; (2-4) three Miami-Dade or Broward SMMC-LTC personal-care and attendant-care agencies; (5-6) two Florida nurse registries; (7-8) two homemaker and companion providers; (9) one pediatric private-duty-nursing or home-health agency (Medicaid under 21, higher dollars per claim); (10) one Florida home-health billing firm as a channel partner. Pricing has to be a flat or per-packet fee, because a percentage of recovery is barred. Expect 14 or more weeks, because a BAA and data access come before any paid month.
G:mhc_revenue:3.deciding_reason: The freight model's engine, a percentage of recovered dollars, is barred for Medicaid claim work in Florida (Fla. Stat. 409.913(10)) and federally (42 CFR 447.10(f)). What remains legal is a flat-fee subscription in a niche where HHAeXchange (the EVV gatekeeper, claiming 99.9% Florida first-pass), GEOH ($30M+ raised) and Claim Health (YC, $4.4M seed) already sell it. My own estimate of the Florida payer-fault recoverable pool is $10-45M a year. That means a $1-4M ceiling at legal pricing, nowhere near $10M. The MHC Area LLCs in the NPI registry are Choice Health at Home (PE-backed, Medicare Advantage), so the family pilot is not established.

sharpened.title: Contract-to-Cash Match for private-contract home care payers (Florida first)
sharpened.one_liner: Match authorization, delivered visits, contract rate and remittance for home care payers where a contingency fee is legal (Medicare Advantage, commercial, VA community care), and recover payer-fault underpayments for a share of what is recovered.
sharpened.pitch:
As written, Triple-Match for Florida Medicaid is dead. Fla. Stat. 409.913(10) and 42 CFR 447.10(f) bar paying anyone who helps prepare Medicaid claims a percentage of what is recovered, and the legal alternative is a thin flat-fee subscription. HHAeXchange (the EVV gatekeeper), GEOH ($30M+ raised) and Claim Health (YC, $4.4M seed) already sell that. The NPI registry also shows the MHC Area LLCs are Choice Health at Home, a PE-backed Medicare Advantage business, not a proven family pilot.

The only thread that survives keeps the freight audit's mechanics and moves the payer. Take agencies paid under private contracts (Medicare Advantage, commercial, VA community care), where the OIG has said percentage billing arrangements are not illegal per se. Match each authorization to visits delivered to the contracted rate to the remittance. Chase only payer-fault gaps: short pays against contract, visit counts authorized below the plan's own approval, late-pay interest.
